Must-see attractions

Sprawled over 145 square kilometres and surrounded by the mountains of Sierra de Tramuntana, this Spanish municipality’s history dates back to the 13th century, with estates still standing from the 16th and 17th centuries.

Can Verger, which now hosts a library and facilities for young people, and Can Ros are among the best known old Mallorcan manors still standing.

There is also a selection of markets to visit. The traditional market in Calvià village is the city’s oldest and takes place every Monday morning, where more than 60 stalls offer visitors food, clothes and handicrafts.

Calvià has also frequently been the destination of choice for both national and international film productions, including the 2019 comedy “The Hustle”, starring Anne Hathaway and Rebel Wilson. Filming took place across various locations, including Puerto Portals.

Several certified hiking trails are ideal for exploring Calvià on foot.

NATO fighter jets and a Latvian interceptor drone were deployed overnight after an unidentified drone briefly entered the country's airspace near the Russian border, Latvia's National Armed Forces (NBS) said on Friday.

"Fighter jets from NATO's air-policing mission in the Baltic States were scrambled, and an interceptor drone from the national armed forces was deployed," the army said. The interceptor returned to its launch site after the flight, and air defence units were ready to respond immediately.

The NBS did not say where the drone came from. It said it had sent extra air defence units to the eastern border, and warned that foreign drones could again enter Latvian airspace while Russia's war in Ukraine continues.

Several countries near the war have reported drone incursions or crashes since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Consumer prices fell by 0.7% in November 2026, after rising by 0.4% in October, according to the latest figures from Insee, published this Friday.

Prices fell by 0.7% in November after rising by 0.4% in October, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies (Insee) said on Friday.

This slowdown in inflation is largely explained by the movement in energy prices. While they are still showing a sharp increase compared with last year, they rose at a less rapid pace in November than in October, moving from +24,1 % to +19,2 %.

Insee particularly highlights the marked fall in prices of petroleum products, even though gas tariffs continue to rise.

Service inflation also fell back to 2,3 % year-on-year, after 2,6 % in October, a drop that Insee attributes to a "sharp slowdown" in prices for accommodation and transport.

By contrast, Insee records a slight increase in food prices (up 1,3 % over one year after 1,2 % in October), driven by a sharp rise in the fresh products sector (+9,4 % over one year compared with 8 % in October).

Consumption and unemployment stable

Meanwhile, French household spending on goods stabilised this month, after falling in September and August, according to Insee.

The drop in energy consumption (-2,9%) is offset by a rebound in consumption of manufactured goods (+1,3%), while food consumption remains stable (-0,1%).

The report also highlights the stability of salaried employment (0,0 %, that is -12 200 jobs, compared with -0,1 %, or -26 100 jobs, in the previous quarter). However, employment figures continue to fall year-on-year for the fifth consecutive quarter.

Salaried employment nonetheless clearly exceeds its level before the health crisis at the end of 2019 (+4,8 %, that is +1,2 million jobs), the national statistics institute notes.

However, France's gross domestic product (GDP) fell by 0,2 % in volume in the third quarter of 2026, after remaining stable in the previous quarter, Insee says, adding that the growth carry-over for 2026 stands at +0,1 %.

The purchasing power of households' gross disposable income (RDB) per consumption unit rose by 0,2 % (after a fall of 0,5 %), while the household saving rate stabilised in the third quarter at 17,4 % of their RDB.

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde with eurozone inflation at twice the ECB’s target. Analysts expect broad policy continuity, but say he could take a more direct role in shaping interest-rate decisions.

European leaders have backed Spain’s former central bank chief, Pablo Hernández de Cos, to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank, which sets interest rates for the eurozone, home to 359 million people.

This comes as the eurozone faces high inflation driven by the Iran war, and concerns over high government debt and borrowing costs across Europe.

Leaders from the 21 EU countries that use the euro also backed candidates for two other top posts at the ECB.

Hernández de Cos is currently general manager of the Bank for International Settlements, which is dubbed the central bank of central banks, in Basel, Switzerland. He served on the ECB’s rate-setting Governing Council from 2018 to 2024 as head of Spain’s central bank and has a reputation for backing lower interest rates and monetary stimulus.

Hernández de Cos built a reputation in Spain as a consensus builder. Analysts expect him to bring that approach to the ECB while taking a more active role than Lagarde in shaping monetary policy.

Andrew Kenningham, chief Europe economist at Capital Economics, told Euronews Business that "Pablo Hernández de Cos is an economists’ economist". He described him as "technically highly competent and respected" and said he takes an interest in the details of monetary policy.

Kenningham does not expect him to change the course of monetary policy much in the near term, "but he will be more likely to challenge advice from the Chief Economist than his predecessor".

Kenningham sees Hernández de Cos as leaning towards lower rates, in line with Capital Economics' forecast that the ECB may raise rates by just another quarter of a percentage point before starting to cut them by the end of 2027.

Eurozone inflation was 4% in October, above the bank’s 2% target. The ECB could still raise rates on 17 December, when Christine Lagarde will chair the meeting.

How Hernández de Cos might steer the ECB

ING's global head of macro, Carsten Brezski, told Euronews Business that he expected Hernández de Cos to play a more hands-on role. "We will now get a president (again) who will leave a clearer personal mark on monetary policy than his predecessor."

Brezski said he expected Hernández de Cos to continue building consensus on the Governing Council, as Lagarde had, while taking a more active role in shaping policy. He said investors would pay closer attention to the president’s speeches for clues about where interest rates were headed.

A review of his speeches by Commerzbank analysts “suggests that de Cos is among the monetary policy doves,” or policymakers who lean toward lower rates to support growth.

In 2020, Hernández de Cos backed the ECB’s pandemic bond-buying programme, which was expanded to €1.85 trillion. It helped keep borrowing costs down as closures and travel restrictions hit the economy. In a speech that year, he said the programme “has been clearly successful in curbing financial market deterioration in all euro area countries” and had lowered borrowing costs for eurozone governments and companies.

Commerzbank analyst Marco Wagner said that “especially against the backdrop of rising government debt in numerous countries ... many governments are likely to prefer a dovish ECB president.” France in particular is struggling with high debt and rising interest costs.

Brezski sees Hernández de Cos as a pragmatist. "It’s hard to put De Cos into the dove-hawk category. In my view, he will simply be a very pragmatic central banker."

Two other seats on the ECB board

Hernández de Cos won out over another leading contender, former Dutch central bank head Klaas Knot, who was regarded as a hawk, or someone who favours higher rates to ward off inflation.

The European Council also put forward France’s Laurence Boone, who heads Santander’s corporate and investment banking business in France, and Germany’s Markus Brunnermeier, a professor at Princeton University, for two seats on the ECB’s six-member executive board.

Brezski said France appeared to have played a key role in securing backing for Hernández de Cos. "It seems as if the French were key, shifting their support from Knot to De Cos." He suggested France may have put more weight on securing the role held by Isabel Schnabel, who oversees market operations, including the implementation of any future bond purchases.

The ECB can buy bonds in certain circumstances to bring down government borrowing costs when it judges that market turmoil is unwarranted and threatens the way monetary policy works across the eurozone. Analysts say the bank is unlikely to step in if France’s borrowing costs rise because its politicians cannot agree on how to cut the deficit.

Kenningham sees Boone as more likely to favour lower rates than Isabel Schnabel, whom she would replace. He sees Brunnermeier as more likely to favour higher rates than Philip Lane, whom he would replace.

"The net impact on policy will probably therefore be small, though it remains to be seen what positions they take up when they are in post", he said.

The European Parliament and the ECB’s Governing Council will be consulted on all three candidates before EU leaders make the formal appointments.

Lagarde is leaving before her term ends

Lagarde, 70, announced on 29 October that she would step down on 7 February 2027, around nine months before the end of her eight-year term. She has said she decided to leave early so she could speak more freely about issues beyond monetary policy.

As for her plans, in an exclusive interview with Euronews, Lagarde said in July that she was "not a candidate for anything", playing down speculation that she might run in France’s presidential election.

In October, she declined to say whether she would back a candidate or what job she would take next. However, in November, Lagarde said a leadership role at the World Economic Forum was “one of the options” after she leaves the ECB. She already sits on the forum’s board of trustees.

Lagarde is regarded as having taken a pragmatic approach, building consensus among the national central bank governors who sit on the rate-setting council. She resisted being labelled a hawk or a dove, saying she was an “owl,” the bird associated with wisdom in Greek and Roman mythology.

She congratulated Hernández de Cos on Thursday, praising his “intellect, warmth and good humour” in a note posted online.

“If he is confirmed, I know these qualities will serve him well as ECB President,” she said.

Europe may be home to three of the world’s fashion capitals, but it has just six cities in Time Out’s top 20 shopping destinations ranking, with only London and Copenhagen making the top 10.

For many of us, a trip to a new place isn’t complete without a little shopping. Around the world, tourists love to snap up a bargain which provides a long-lasting memory after the holiday is over.

Now, Time Out has ranked the best global shopping destinations, with Shanghai in China taking the top spot.

Despite being the home to three out of the “big four” fashion capitals, Europe only has six entries in the top 20, and just two – London and Copenhagen – are in the top 10.

That was decided by a combination of Time Out’s global network of editors, local experts and data from the publication’s annual Best Cities survey, which gathered the views of more than 24,000 local residents across 150 cities worldwide.

The scoring model combines 70% local sentiment and 30% expert evaluation, based on five key pillars:

  • quality and variety of shopping, affordability, city vibe
  • how safe and welcoming locals consider their city
  • wider city experience
  • the quality of restaurants, public transport and walkability
  • expert evaluation, which is made up of Time Out editors’ assessment of each city’s shopping offering in 2026

These are the best cities for shopaholics to add to their bucket list.

Shanghai, China

Shanghai’s shopping scene is a mix of international names and a growing crop of homegrown fashion and lifestyle brands.

From rummaging for antiques at Juqi Antique City to browsing beauty boutiques along Anfu Road and exploring immersive retail spaces on Middle Huaihai Road, there’s plenty to discover.

Local labels including An Ko Rau, The Beast, Pane and Short Sentence are among Time Out’s recommendations.

London, United Kingdom

One of the four main fashion capitals – alongside Paris, New York and Milan – London is world-renowned for a hugely varied shopping scene.

It certainly caters to all tastes, from the famous department stores of Harrods, Liberty and Selfridges to the vintage shops of Brick Lane, designer boutiques on Bond Street and independent record stores in Soho.

For something quintessentially British, Time Out recommends stopping by the original Daunt Books in Marylebone, just north of shopping paradise Oxford Street.

Tokyo, Japan

It seems like Japan is on everyone’s must-visit list, judging by the number of viral shopping haul videos on social media.

That’s no surprise as Tokyo’s shopping districts offer everything from high-end fashion and vintage designer finds to quirky stationery, manga, cute trinkets and traditional crafts.

Ginza is the place for luxury labels and grand department stores, while Harajuku, Shibuya and Omotesando have a mix of independent boutiques and trend-led brands.

For vintage shopping, head to Shimokitazawa or Koenji, or visit Beams Japan for a curated selection of Japanese fashion, design and crafts.

New York City, United States

New York is the only non-European fashion capital, and its shopping credentials are legendary, far beyond Fifth Avenue and its iconic department stores.

Across the five boroughs, shoppers can discover independent designers, rare vinyl, vintage fashion, antiques, artisan goods and specialist retailers.

Time Out recommends Grand Bazaar on the Upper West Side, the city’s longest-running market, for discovering local makers and taking home a unique piece of the Big Apple.

Melbourne, Australia

Melbourne’s shops reflect the city’s creative, independent spirit, with everything from international labels and luxury fashion in the Central Business District (CBD) and Chadstone to vintage finds and emerging designers in Fitzroy and Collingwood.

Armadale’s High Street is a good place to discover Australian fashion, while beauty fans should make a beeline for Mecca’s flagship on Bourke Street.

The two countries want TikTok’s European business and key technology, including its recommendation algorithm, to come under European control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address security concerns.

Germany and Austria on Thursday called for TikTok's European business to be placed under European ownership and control, arguing that regulation alone cannot address concerns over data access and algorithms.

The Chinese-owned social media platform poses "fundamental security policy risks for Europe", German culture and media minister Wolfram Weimer said after meeting Austrian digital state secretary Alexander Proell in Vienna.

In a joint statement, the two politicians called for "a European ownership structure for TikTok's European business and European responsibility for the key technological infrastructure — from the recommendation algorithm to data access".

Germany and Austria will seek to build EU-wide support for their proposal at a meeting of the Telecommunications and Energy (TTE) Council in Brussels on December 2, the statement said.

On November 6, TikTok was preliminarily found to be in breach of Europe's Digital Services Act (DSA) over how its recommender system exposes users to potentially harmful content.

But Weimer and Proell said regulation did not answer "the basic question of who actually controls the platform".

"TikTok is no longer a toy, but part of the infrastructure of our democracy. This infrastructure must not remain in the hands of a geopolitical systemic rival," Proell said.

ByteDance, the Chinese parent company of TikTok, in January ceded control of the platform's US operations to a majority American-owned joint venture, in response to a threatened ban in the United States.

Weimer in May said he was "firmly convinced that Europe should follow the American example and that the company's ownership structure must be put up for discussion".

TikTok rejected the proposal as having "zero merit", saying it ignored existing European laws including the Digital Services Act and GDPR as well as the company's 12-billion-euro Project Clover data security programme.

TikTok also said its European operations are run by companies incorporated in Ireland and Britain and are subject to European law, while parent company ByteDance is majority-owned by global institutional investors and has no Chinese government ownership stake.

An 18-year-old has been detained over the latest breach of Denmark’s national civil registry, two months after a separate cyberattack exposed data linked to 8.8 million people.

An 18-year-old has been arrested in connection to a cyber-attack that leaked the personal information of 11,000 people from Denmark's national registry, authorities said Thursday, two months after another huge data hack.

Danish authorities said they had updated and modernised security systems since the early October attack, when the data of 8.8 million people was illegally accessed.

Despite that "the administration of the Civil Registration System (CPR) has discovered a new security breach," the digital affairs ministry said.

"Unauthorised third parties have accessed the CPR data of 11,000 people," it said, adding that the breach was detected on November 23.

The incident "was stopped thanks to a new technical monitoring system for consultations, introduced after the first incident."

An 18-year-old man has been arrested and remanded in custody "for having, without authorisation, accessed the Civil Registration System, where he managed to retrieve 11,000 identification numbers," police said in a statement.

The perpetrators of the October hack have not been identified yet.

But in October, an unidentified person contacted Danish newspaper Politiken in English via an encrypted messaging service and claimed responsibility.

The supposed hacker said they had found an entry point into the register within a few hours by using the login credentials of a former employee of a small Danish company.

They said the employee's password was 123456.

In September, the Civil Security Agency raised the threat level for cyberattacks against Denmark to "high".

There has been a surge in cyberattacks, notably targeting supermarket refrigeration systems.

There has also been a series of false bomb threats against schools and planes across Europe, which could potentially be part of a hybrid warfare campaign.

That theory has not been confirmed, however, due to a lack of evidence.

Good morning. Leo Cendrowicz here with your Friday newsletter. They rush in, elbow each other out of the way, squabble over the price and emerge with precious little to show for it. But enough about Black Friday - we also have an angry EU summit to report on…

A summit to forget. Fourteen hours of talks, a boycott, a French presidential ultimatum, a bruised European Council president and virtually nothing to show for it. Yesterday’s special EU summit, convened specifically to break the deadlock over the bloc’s next seven-year budget, ended shortly after midnight in spectacular disarray. Leaders abandoned plans to continue negotiations today and went home, seemingly no closer to a deal than when they arrived.

As our Jorge Liboreiro and Luca Bertuzzi report, the summit was practically doomed from the outset. European Council President António Costa’s €1.78 trillion compromise, shaving €204 billion off the Commission’s original proposal, achieved the remarkable feat of antagonising almost everyone.

The great walkout. The seven so-called frugals – Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, Finland and now Belgium – want deeper cuts and spending redirected towards defence, innovation and competitiveness. The 17 Friends of Cohesion want to protect traditional spending on poorer regions and agriculture.

Costa tried to shake things up by breaking leaders into smaller, geographically mixed groups. Instead, the frugals decided they were being unfairly targeted and boycotted the format. Costa carried on without them.

“We had a lot of physical movement, with all the meetings, but we did not really see any movement on content,” one diplomat told us.

The science of disagreement. With Italy’s Giorgia Meloni describing a deal as “light years away” and Hungary’s Péter Magyar putting the chances of an agreement at “pretty much zero”, you could be forgiven for thinking we were covering a conference of particle physicists rather than a gathering of European leaders.

Meanwhile, Emmanuel Macron decided what the summit really needed was more Emmanuel Macron. Breaking away from the negotiations to hold his own press conference, the French president cast himself as the great European dealmaker. “I'm trying to bring everyone closer together,” he declared.

His method? Threatening to shut down negotiations after 31 December. The implicit warning: his colleagues might find themselves negotiating with Marine Le Pen instead.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, unimpressed, pointed out that there were 27 bridge-builders, not just one. The Franco-German engine is not exactly purring.

The clock is ticking. Leaders will try again on 17 December, but several seem remarkably relaxed about the timetable. “For me, there's no deadline,” said Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten. Yet the new budget must be operational by January 2028, Parliament still has to approve it, and next year’s electoral cycle could make the political arithmetic considerably uglier.

Remember Ukraine? The other supposedly urgent item on yesterday’s agenda – a €45 billion loan to keep Ukraine afloat next year – was largely swallowed up by the budget brawl. Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic are still refusing to participate. That, too, has been kicked into December.

Productive dysfunction? There is an old Brussels theory that leaders need to exhaust themselves, trade insults and demonstrate to domestic audiences that they have fought tooth and nail before they can make concessions.

“You need to have a bad European Council to have a good one,” one diplomat told us. “It was a lot of political theatre.”

By that logic, December’s summit ought to be an absolute triumph.

In other news

From Madrid to Frankfurt. There was one concrete result from the summit yesterday: Pablo Hernández de Cos was confirmed as the next president of the European Central Bank, becoming the first Spaniard to land the job. But perhaps his most remarkable achievement is to have earned the trust of both Spain’s conservatives and socialists – no mean feat in the country’s fiercely polarised political climate.

The 55-year-old economist is the consummate technocrat. Appointed governor of the Bank of Spain by Mariano Rajoy’s conservative government in 2018, he was subsequently championed for the ECB presidency by Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist administration.

Currently heading the Bank for International Settlements, Hernández de Cos has spent much of his career navigating the intricacies of monetary policy, banking supervision and financial stability. He is regarded as an orthodox economist, broadly aligned with the ECB’s hawks, although he advocated interest rate cuts in 2024. Expect a steady hand rather than fireworks in Frankfurt.

Spain’s right turn? Conspicuously absent from the EU summit, Pedro Sánchez is fighting for his political survival as Spaniards go to the polls on Sunday. He joined three other party leaders last night in a televised debate. His widely anticipated defeat would rob the EU of its highest-profile centre-left leader and further tilt the bloc’s political balance to the right. Polls suggest the conservative Popular Party will need the Vox party to govern, bringing the far right into national government for the first time since Spain’s democratic transition.

The price of solidarity. How can the EU afford another €45 billion loan to Ukraine? Our Euronews Verify team crunches the numbers: the money would be borrowed on financial markets, backed by the EU budget rather than national balance sheets. Bruegel economist Jacob Funk Kirkegaard reckons the sum, equivalent to just 0.2% of EU GDP, is modest compared with the potential cost of defending Europe should Russia prevail in Ukraine.

Gulf tensions. Two Italian technicians working for German defence giant Rheinmetall were killed in a strike on a facility in Kuwait, prompting Rome and Kuwait City to blame Iran. Tehran denied responsibility, describing the incident as suspicious. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called for increased pressure on Iran, warning that Gulf security was a concern for everyone. The deaths come amid growing fears of renewed escalation in the conflict.

Bardella under fire. French far-right leader Jordan Bardella has denied fresh allegations of antisemitism after Le Monde and Mediapart published further messages he allegedly wrote as a teenager, including conspiracy theories about Jewish control of banks. Bardella denounced a media “persecution” campaign. The revelations are awkward for the National Rally, which has spent years trying to shed its antisemitic past and court Jewish voters.

Buyer beware. EU Justice Commissioner Michael McGrath has warned Black Friday shoppers against bogus discounts and pressure-selling tactics. Checks last year found that 30% of online shops surveyed provided misleading discount information. McGrath’s proposed Digital Fairness Act would crack down on hidden fees, fake countdown timers and subscription traps. “A genuine deal should never depend on misleading the consumer,” he said.

Brexit break-up bill. Britain’s new food and drink deal with the EU comes with an exit penalty: either side walking away within 10 years would have to cover the costs of restoring border checks. The clause looks like an insurance policy against another reversal in British politics. Reform UK’s Nigel Farage has already vowed to repeal Andy Burnham’s Brexit reset, while Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has also opposed the deal.

Fashion house Armani is stepping up its hospitality ambitions, with new luxury hotels planned in Saudi Arabia and Egypt.

Currently, the Italian luxury brand has properties in Dubai and Milan – where it was founded – but it’s decided to expand some distance from Italy’s fashion capital.

Instead, it has announced plans for its first hotel in Egypt, a beachfront development on the Red Sea scheduled to open in 2030. That announcement follows the ongoing construction of Armani Hotel Diriyah in Riyadh, which is expected to welcome its first guests in 2027.

The upcoming openings are part of a much bigger plan to grow Armani's presence in the luxury hospitality market.

At present, the brand operates two hotels: Armani Hotel Dubai, which occupies several floors of the Burj Khalifa, and Armani Hotel Milano.

The Dubai property opened in 2010, followed by the Milan hotel in 2011. Both were developed through Armani's long-standing partnership with businessman Mohamed Alabbar, founder of real estate development company Emaar.

In January 2026, the two parties announced a new joint venture through Alabbar's private investment company, Symphony Global, giving the partnership worldwide exclusivity to develop future Armani Hotels & Resorts in selected international destinations.

The agreement runs for 20 years, with an option to extend it by a further decade.

There have been rumours of potential future destinations for hotels and resorts, including London, Paris, New York, Miami, Bangkok, Singapore, Tokyo and the Maldives.

Here’s what we know so far about the confirmed upcoming openings.

Expansion into Saudi Arabia amid a tourism boom

Currently under construction in Diriyah, a historic area on the outskirts of Riyadh, Armani Hotel Diriyah is scheduled to open sometime in 2027.

The development forms part of the wider Diriyah project, one of Saudi Arabia's major tourism and cultural regeneration schemes, which is centred around the historic At-Turaif District, a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The district’s traditional Najdi architecture, mud-brick buildings and narrow streets are a world away from Riyadh's modern skyscrapers.

The new hotel will bring Armani's design-led approach to this historic setting, adding another luxury accommodation option, among many already existing and soon to be opened, for visitors exploring the area.

Armani Hotels to make Egyptian debut on the Red Sea

Scheduled to open in 2030, Armani is planning a new hotel and residential development at Marassi Red Sea, a coastal resort and residential development near Hurghada International Airport.

The beachfront property will overlook both the Red Sea and the marina, bringing together hotel accommodation, serviced apartments and a limited collection of private residences carrying the Armani name.

Interiors will follow the aesthetic of Armani/Casa, the fashion house's furniture and interior design arm, with the brand promising its signature understated style and attention to detail throughout.

Wellness will also be a major part of the offering here. Plans include a dedicated sanctuary focused on health, restoration and longevity, with personalised treatments, fitness facilities and relaxation experiences.

The number of new HIV diagnoses has fallen over the past year, but late diagnoses remain a challenge in Greece.

New HIV diagnoses in Greece have fallen year-over-year, but challenges remain, preliminary health data shows.

As of October, 490 new cases were recorded this year in the National HIV Registry, corresponding to 4.7 diagnoses per 100,000 population.

New diagnoses are at lower levels than in the same period of 2025, according to data from the National Public Health Organisation (EODY).

Despite the decline, there are significant challenges for timely diagnosis and epidemiological surveillance. Roughly half of the cases for which data were available were diagnosed at a late stage, and authorities don't know how the infection spread in a significant proportion of cases.

According to EODY data, 22,408 HIV infection cases have been recorded through October 2026. Among those cases, 5,200 people developed AIDS and 3,980 died. Meanwhile, 11,891 HIV patients received antiretroviral therapy (ART) to suppress their viral loads.

As for the new diagnoses, 84.1% were among men and 15.9% were among women.

Unprotected sexual contact continues to be the main way HIV spreads in Greece. Among the 490 new diagnoses, 41.6% concerned men who had unprotected sexual contact with men. Another 12.7% were linked to unprotected heterosexual sex, while 10.6% were linked to shared needles and other intravenous drug use.

However, the number of cases for which the transmission route is undefined or has not been filled in remains particularly high. This concerns 169 diagnoses, which represent 34.5% of the total.

One of the most important findings of the epidemiological report concerns late diagnosis of HIV infection. Among 281 new diagnoses that could be assessed, roughly half were made in a later stage.

Among people aged 40-49 the rate of late diagnosis reached 57.3%, while in the 50-and-over age group it rose to 62.5%. By contrast, lower rates were recorded among men who had sexual contact with men (41%) and among people aged 30-39 (34.7%).

The report also records a shift in the age distribution of new cases. While up to 2024 the 30-39 age group predominated, over the past two years people in their 40s have been the most frequent diagnoses. At the same time, in recent years there has been an increase in the proportion of diagnoses among people over 50.

Overall, 30.2% of new diagnoses were made among people in their 40s, followed by people in their 30s at 25.9% and people aged 50 and over at 22.9%.

Among the positive findings of the report is the decrease in new cases linked to the shared use of intravenous drugs.

Specifically, in 2026 a reduction of 22.4% was recorded compared with 2025. However, EODY emphasises that levels have not yet returned to those before the epidemic surge that occurred in the period 2011-2013.

Changes to solar incentives and long installation processes mean European homeowners could benefit from planning now.

Winter is cold, dark and grey. Yet for many Europeans, it’s a great time to switch to solar power.

While many are focused on the holiday season, industry experts are urging homeowners considering a switch to solar to contact suppliers before Christmas – although not to take advantage of the winter sun.

Several European countries are making changes to solar energy subsidies and tax breaks in 2027, meaning homeowners might want to fast-track their plans to enjoy the financial benefits.

But even without changes to government incentives, there are good reasons to get ahead of the spring sunshine.

How long does it take to install solar panels?

Although a typical rooftop solar installation takes just one or two days, getting building permits and, in some cases, approval to connect to electricity grids can take weeks. Sometimes months.

Last year, an OECD report citing earlier research found that permit times for rooftop solar projects ranged from six weeks in Malta to as many as 10 months in Bulgaria.

The country has since made it easier for homeowners, scrapping permit requirements for solar systems up to 20 kilowatts intended for personal use, but delays are still common across Europe.

In Germany, a consumer watchdog warned last year that homeowners in Saxony were waiting months to have their solar panels connected to the grid – and, in extreme cases, more than a year.

And Edward Gurney, the founding director of the UK-based Solar and Battery Company, says getting approval from electricity providers can take four to five weeks even under normal circumstances.

“A lot of solar equipment is manufactured in China, and getting replacement stock delivered can take around six weeks,” he says.

Winter weather can also disrupt installation schedules, as icy roofs make working conditions unsafe.

“When you’ve already got a busy installation schedule, losing even a few days to bad weather can push subsequent installations back,” Gurney says.

Why it pays to install solar panels before spring

Waiting until the weather warms up could mean missing out on a prime period for solar production, too.

Solar power generated less than five per cent of the EU’s electricity in January last year, but by May, it was supplying more than 20 per cent, according to the European Environment Agency.

In Germany alone, 74 per cent of the solar electricity fed into the grid last year was generated between April and September.

The sooner homeowners have their panels installed, the sooner they can start benefitting from this springtime bump.

In the meantime, Gurney recommends using winter to assess how much electricity you might use and compare quotations from different installers.

“The number of panels, battery capacity and how much electricity your household uses will all affect the long-term value of the installation,” he says.

Solar subsidies are changing across Europe

Homeowners in several European countries could face changes to the cost of installing solar panels in 2027. Since April 2022, homeowners in England, Scotland and Wales have been able to have solar panels installed without paying value-added tax. From 1 April 2027, the tax rate will return to five per cent.

In Germany, people who install solar panels from January onward could miss out on government support unless new energy laws are approved before the end of the year, the German Solar Industry Association warns.

Although German lawmakers have tentatively agreed to continue paying homeowners for surplus electricity they sell to the grid from solar systems up to 25 kilowatts, they have yet to strike a final deal.

And in Austria, the government plans to stop offering grants for solar panels in 2027 and instead help homeowners buy batteries to store the electricity they generate.

In the UK, at least, the looming tax hike appears to be prompting consumers to act. The Solar and Battery Company reported a 37 per cent bump in enquiries about solar installations in early November as UK residents seek to beat the April deadline.

Gurney expects demand to continue growing as the deadline nears, but he also warns that booking an installation before April doesn’t guarantee homeowners will avoid having to pay the tax.

Most drug-related ER visits in a new survey involved people who had taken more than one drug or mixed drugs with alcohol.

Cocaine sent more people to the emergency room than any other drug in 2025, according to a new analysis of select hospitals from the European Union Drugs Agency.

Nearly 14,700 people sought emergency medical help for drug overdoses or other “acute drug-toxicity” at surveyed hospitals in 2025, the agency said. That includes both illegal drugs and misused prescription medications. The analysis dug into about 7,400 of these cases at 45 hospitals across 18 EU member states and Norway.

Cocaine was involved in 32% of ER visits, followed by cannabis (24%) and amphetamine (11%). In all, 39% of visits involved a single drug, while 23% involved a drug and alcohol and 38% involved multiple substances.

For example, 72% of patients who visited the ER about ketamine had also been drinking or used another drug, the report found. The most common combination was cannabis, cocaine and alcohol.

“Polysubstance use is more the norm than the exception,” said Isabelle Giraudon, the EUDA’s principal scientist on the health consequences of drug use.

That is worrisome because some drugs interact in ways that “cause additional problems and increase the risk of severe outcomes,” Giraudon told Euronews.

For example, she said people who take opioids or GHB/GBL (gamma-hydroxybutyrate/gamma-butyrolactone) — sometimes called “G” or “liquid ecstasy” — along with alcohol, benzodiazepines or other depressants may be at higher risk of respiratory slowdown, which can become life-threatening.

Patients who took a single drug, or a single drug and alcohol, spent a median of five hours in the hospital, compared with seven hours for people who took at least two drugs, the analysis found.

Overall, 66% of patients were medically discharged directly from the ER — but that varied depending on the drug they had used. Patients who used methamphetamine or amphetamines were more likely to be referred to a psychiatric ward than people who took other drugs.

Meanwhile, people on heroin or GHB/GBL were more likely to be sent to a critical care unit.

Younger people were more likely to visit the ER for ecstasy or nitrous oxide, commonly known as laughing gas, while the median age was 38 for visits involving heroin and 36 for crack cocaine.

Men accounted for 72% of hospital visits, which peaked on weekends. Two-thirds of patients arrived by ambulance.

While there were big differences across European hospitals, this type of data can help “inform the local policy and responses, based on the local situation and needs, and improve preparedness,” Giraudon said.

Notably, the analysis only included drug poisoning patients who made it to the ER, not those who died of an overdose or were treated on site and did not go to the hospital. It also did not track health complications from regular drug use, such as infected injection sites or hepatitis B, a liver infection that spreads through blood and bodily fluids.

“This data represent only a fraction of drug-related harms,” Giraudon said.

Trip.com has ranked Europe’s best family-friendly attractions for 2027, with Disneyland Paris at number one and London landmarks dominating the top 10.

Keeping the whole family entertained while on holiday is no easy feat. Fortunately, there is no shortage of attractions in Europe that cater to travellers of all ages.

For families already planning where to go in the year ahead, Trip.com has compiled its 2027 Europe 50 Family-friendly Attractions ranking, which is based on “genuine customer reviews, year-round sales popularity, consistent quality assurance and distinctive themes”.

The best attractions were chosen for search popularity, thematic relevance, duration on the rankings and ranking position, with the family-friendly attractions being defined as those that offer “facilities and services, ensuring a safe, fun and educational experience”.

Disneyland Paris, which scored 4.7/5 across 4,177 reviews, has been recognised as Trip’s top family-friendly attraction for 2027. Having achieved a four-year streak on the platform’s annual lists, it offers families a getaway with parades and performances for children, alongside services for parents within its parks and hotels.

UK destinations dominated the list, with half of the entries within the top 10, including the iconic London Eye and Warner Bros Studio Tour London on the outskirts of the capital.

In the Netherlands, the water village of Giethoorn emerged in fifth place and offers families a quiet getaway known for its historic canals, narrow waterways and being car-free. Visitors can hop on a kayak, board a canal cruise or hire a “sloop”, which is a small electric boat ideal for sailing across the canals.

Ranked seventh, City Park in Budapest, Hungary, is a green escape that’s home to many species of plants and animals. Across 13,000 square metres, the main playground offers children ample space for play.

Pena Park in Sintra, Portugal, makes its first appearance on Trip’s annual lists. It ranked ninth overall and features winding, labyrinthine paths that weave beneath its dense woodland before arriving at the National Palace of Pena.

Rounding off the top 10 is Kalemegdan Park in Belgrade, Serbia. The cultural monument covers more than 60 hectares and features archaeological sites for history buffs.

New Zealand's final vote count has left neither bloc with a majority, handing a brand-new centrist party the power to decide who governs.

The Electoral Commission's final tally showed more support for minor parties on the ideological flanks than before. A total of 2.8 million votes were cast.

The tally on Friday, after 400,000 special votes including ballots from New Zealanders abroad, showed Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's National party dropping two seats to finish on 40.

The right-wing bloc now holds 65 seats in the 130-seat parliament, one short of the 66 needed. The left, led by Labour's Chris Hipkins, has 58, with Labour on 36.

That leaves the Opportunity party, an unaligned centrist newcomer with seven seats, as kingmaker. Its support would not be enough to put the left in power, Hipkins conceded on Friday, in an apparent admission of defeat.

Luxon, who ruled out working with Opportunity before the 7 November vote, reversed course saying he was confident of forming a government with Opportunity and his usual partners, the libertarian ACT (13 seats) and the populist NZ First (12).

All three minor parties would need to back him.

"These negotiations may be challenging and they could take some time," he said. "But getting it right matters far more than getting it done quickly."

Qiulae Wong, the 38-year-old newcomer

Opportunity is led by 38-year-old business consultant Qiulae Wong, who has said she could work with either side. Her party's five "bottom line" policies include tougher climate action and an end to bottom-trawling, both at odds with ACT and NZ First.

Wong also repeated that she will not join a government in which NZ First leader Winston Peters is foreign minister, citing his past remarks in parliament about Asian people. She said she would consider either a full coalition or a "confidence and supply" deal, under which her MPs would back key legislation and decide other bills case by case.

Both major parties took under 30% of the party vote: Labour 29.88% and National 28.35%. Analysts pointed to anger over the cost of living and little enthusiasm for either leader.

PM Luxon survived two confidence votes among his own MPs this year, while Hipkins led Labour to defeat in 2023. Minor parties on both flanks gained ground, with the Greens on 17 seats and Te Pati Māori on five.

Chosen by the Popular Party to head the Bank of Spain in 2018 and backed by Pedro Sánchez's PSOE for the ECB presidency, Hernández de Cos is widely regarded as an orthodox economist with an impeccable civil service career.

In a country with levels of polarisation comparable to those of Brazil or the United States, Pablo Hernández de Cos (Madrid, 1971) appears to have worked a miracle in Spain: he has emerged as a figure of consensus and, for a brief moment, interrupted the fratricidal struggle between socialists and the conservative populares who hope to win back the Palacio de la Moncloa at the election this Sunday.

The first Spaniard who will preside over the European Central Bank is a well-known figure in the country's public sphere, and also one of the few citizens who can boast, together with Felipe VI and Letizia de Borbón, of having been portrayed by the leading photographer of the global elites, Annie Leibovitz.

In a clear contrast with the much-discussed portraits that the American took of the monarchs at the time, the artist set out to stage a Hernández de Cos who is approachable but with the authority that emanates from someone posing at the head of the table in the Governing Council chamber of the Bank of Spain, an institution he headed between 2018 and 2024.

His professional milestones always seem to occur just days before Spanish political history changes. This 55-year-old economist was proposed by the previous administration of Mariano Rajoy as governor of the BDE on 28 May 2018; it was one of the former president's last actions.

Four days later, the first successful no-confidence motion of the democratic era led to Rajoy's resignation and the rise to power of the current leader, Pedro Sánchez. After the elections on Sunday 29, it will be seen whether Hernández de Cos's imminent move to Frankfurt, after being confirmed as president of the European Central Bank this Thursday, will once again act as an omen of political change in Spain.

The Hernández family saga: from Suárez to Sánchez

Although he had begun a career as a police officer, the economist's father, Inocencio Hernández Amores, was assigned to La Moncloa in the first year of Spain's return to democracy, in 1978, where he gained the trust of president Adolfo Suárez. Originally from the south of Castile and León, the two hit it off and Hernández senior became the leader's personal secretary.

Hernández de Cos therefore grew up in a middle-class, politicised environment that bore witness to the country's profound changes. Journalist John Müller notes in a 2022 report in 'ABC' that the young economist grew up rebellious, taking part in several demonstrations in the new Spain emerging in the 1980s. It is an image that does not correspond to the grey technocratic facade that the new president of the ECB projects in each of his public appearances, although those who know him describe him as an approachable sort despite his discretion.

Married with two children, Hernández de Cos graduated in Economics and Business Administration from a private university, CUNEF; he obtained his second degree, in Law, at the country's main distance higher education institution, UNED, and finally opted for the public system, at the Complutense University, to earn a doctorate in Economics.

The model civil servant of the transition

A speaker of English and French, a trait not so common among Spaniards of his age, the new doctor rejected academic life or the private sector and sat the entrance exams for what has, until now, been the institution of his life, the Bank of Spain, BDE. He joined it in 1997, at barely 25, as a graduate in its Research Department. It was his second option, since he also sat the exams to become a commercial expert and state economist.

Within the BDE, where he has spent half his professional life, he has held various positions. He has been director general for Economics, Statistics and Research and has sat on the boards of the International Centre for Monetary and Banking Studies and the Foundation for Applied Economic Studies. In that institution he has worked on topics that are macroeconomic, as well as on fiscal and monetary policy and financial stability.

The general consensus among specialists is that Hernández de Cos will maintain orthodox positions aligned with the 'hawks' of the European Central Bank (contrary to the stereotypes usually applied to southern Europeans) except on one issue: interest rates, whose cuts he argued for in 2024.

Hernández de Cos took up the post of director general of the Bank for International Settlements on 1 July 2025, after completing his term at the BDE in 2024. The new director of the European Central Bank knows the institution well: in addition to being a member of its Governing Council, as was appropriate for the head of the Iberian arm, from 2019 to 2024 he chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision and the Advisory Technical Committee of the European Systemic Risk Board.

António Costa's attempt to prod EU leaders into ditching their red lines on the budget fell flat on Thursday as talks turned messy and bitter.

A summit specifically convened to find a breakthrough on the European Union's next budget ended in disarray after leaders, split in opposing camps, refused to abandon their red lines and openly questioned whether a deal could be reached by December.

The meeting was plagued by tensions, reproaches and even boycotts, raising serious questions on the leadership of European Council President António Costa, whose credibility now rests on whether these negotiations succeed or fail.

Costa's compromise proposalworth €1.78 trillion in current prices across seven years – a 10% cut from the original draft – was met with fierce pushback from all sides, taking the Council presidency aback.

"This meeting was a necessary step in the process. This is a negotiation process. It is normal that the different parties are starting to underline and mark their starting points. Everybody knows that we cannot fail Europe, and we need to have a new budget from the 1st of January 2028," Costa said at the press conference at the end of the summit.

The summit appeared doomed from the outset.

Leaders showed virtually no willingness to compromise as they made their way into Thursday's gathering and huddled with their respective groups.

On one side, the seven "Frugals", bent on slashing the budget. On the other side, the 17 "Friends of Cohesion", determined to push back against further cuts.

The tone was set by Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, who told reporters upon arrival that a deal on the seven-year budget was "light years away".

Meloni questioned Costa's much-repeated objective of reaching a deal by the end of the year to prevent the process from spilling over into the 2027 electoral cycle.

"I don't have a time limit. I have specific conditions," she said. "When the agreement is one that I consider valid and fair for Italy, then I'll sign it."

Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten, a staunch "frugal", was equally dismissive.

"There's no need to hurry," he said. "For me, there's no deadline."

The budget negotiations began around midday after leaders settled the matter of Christine Lagarde's succession as European Central Bank president. They first met all together in the main room, where they shared their well-known positions.

Nobody caved in during this session, waiting for others to move first, diplomats said.

Then, Costa split the summit into small groups of leaders. First, the "frugals", then the "cohesion friends", and then the six largest member states. After that, he began breakout sessions with geographically mixed leaders.

The proceedings increasingly frustrated the "frugals", who saw it as an attempt to pile pressure on them in favour of the "cohesion friends".

Feeling unfairly targeted, the "frugals" closed ranks and decided to boycott the small-group format, which Costa continued without their participation.

Meanwhile, French President Emmanuel Macron raised the stakes, calling a press conference to deliver a stark ultimatum: reach a deal by December or walk away empty-handed.

Macron warned that protracted negotiations risked becoming dangerously entangled in the French presidential campaign. Far-right firebrand Marine Le Pen, who is leading opinion polls, has vowed to slash France's contribution to the EU budget.

"I intend to make it very clear to our colleagues that, for political and democratic reasons, it will not be possible to reopen or conclude negotiations on the budget after 31st December," Macron said, decrying Costa's proposed cuts as a "strategic mistake".

"We are not prepared to reach a deal at any cost. We can conclude by 31st December, but that is the absolute limit."

Other member states consider Macron's threat of a future Le Pen presidency a tactic to extract concessions and eventually get his way, despite Costa's compromise widely seen as being overly French-friendly.

"That's quite rich," a diplomat quipped about the French reaction.

Macron's mid-summit appearance, a rare occurrence, wiped out chances of a breakthrough and precipitated the collapse of the talks.

In his own press conference, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz adopted a hardline "frugal" stance and vowed to slash the budget even further.

The deep political divide between Paris and Berlin, the EU’s two main powerhouses, has cast a shadow over the negotiations.

"Are we any further ahead? Yes and no. We are trying to define which direction it is going. I think I may say that," Merz told reporters.

The cuts to the budget, he said, will not stop at the €204 billion proposed by Costa. "It will become less," he added. "How much it will be then is open."

The fact that Costa announced early in the summit that the talks would not continue on Friday as originally planned dampened the energy among national delegations and immediately lowered expectations for a breakthrough, a diplomat said.

A second diplomat was more positive on the outcome of the summit, despite the messy proceedings. "You need to have a bad European Council to have a good one," they said. "It was a lot of political theatre. We did not have detailed negotiations."

Forgotten in the talks was Ukraine.

The summit was supposed to discuss a €45 billion support loan for the country, which faces a ballooning wartime deficit amid Russia's relentless attacks. But the budget fight sucked in all the energy and left Ukraine relegated to an afterthought.
